Childcare during asylum interviews

You must not expect parents to give an account of past persecution in front of their children. This is to protect the claimant’s own interests and those of the child, bearing in mind the statutory duty to safeguard and promote the welfare of children. Parents may be reluctant to reveal difficult information with a child present, it may be traumatising for the claimant, or the child and the parent may be distracted whilst trying to look after a child and provide evidence.

Childcare is not available at the interview sites. Interviews of single parents should generally be scheduled when school-age children are attending school. Claimants who are invited to interview who have young children that require childcare and who are unable to make alternative care arrangements, should contact the Home Office using the contact details provided on the invitation to interview to reschedule their interview or seek alternative ways for information to be gathered, for example, by providing a witness statement, questionnaire, or other documentary evidence.

Where no other childcare is available, there may be exceptional circumstances where babies may be present in the room whilst the interview is taking place. For example, the parent would prefer to be present with the child (for example, due to the need to breastfeed), the child is younger than 12 months old, will not be able to understand the content of the interview, and is not distracting to the claimant (for example, because they are napping). If you are unsure, you must seek advice from a Technical Specialist or Senior Caseworker. You must also ensure that you take breaks as appropriate and ensure the wellbeing of everyone in the room.

Whether an interview can proceed in the presence of a baby will depend on the circumstances. In all cases, you must ensure that you are able to conduct a fair and effective asylum interview which will enable the claimant to put forward all relevant information in their case without distraction.

Non-attendance

You must normally require all asylum claimants to attend an interview, except where it may be omitted in accordance with paragraph 339NA of the Immigration Rules. In circumstances where Paragraph 339NA does not apply, the interview will be rescheduled as soon as possible in cases where a claimant provides evidence that they were unable to attend for circumstances beyond their control. It may be appropriate in some circumstances to omit the interview where a claimant is unfit to attend an interview, and it is not possible to reschedule this should be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

Omitting the asylum interview

An interview may be omitted (see paragraph 339NA of the Immigration Rules) where:

you are able to make a decision to grant asylum or humanitarian protection without it

the Home Office has already met with the applicant for the purpose of assisting them with completing their application and submitting the essential information regarding their application

the applicant has only raised issues that are not relevant or of minimal relevance to the examination of whether they are a refugee / eligible for humanitarian protection

the applicant has made inconsistent, contradictory, improbable or insufficient representations which make their claim clearly unconvincing in relation to having been the object of persecution or serious harm

the applicant has submitted a subsequent application which does not raise any relevant new elements with respect to their particular circumstances or to the situation in their country of origin

the applicant is making an application merely in order to delay or frustrate the enforcement of an earlier or imminent decision which would result in their removal

you are of the opinion that it is not reasonably practicable to do so, for example because the applicant is unfit or unable to be interviewed owing to enduring circumstances beyond their control

the applicant is an EU national (whose claim has been determined to be unsuitable for inadmissibility action and instead will be considered substantively)

Non-attendance due to illness

If the claimant is unable to attend or proceed with an interview due to illness or a medical condition, the claimant or their immigration adviser must generally provide a letter or certificate, or another appropriate form of evidence. The evidence must be from a GP, consultant or other appropriately qualified relevant healthcare professional regulated by one of the following regulators:

General Medical Council (GMC)

Health & Care Professions Council (HCPC)

Nursing & Midwifery Council (NMC)

General Dental Council (GDC)

Whilst there may be genuine reasons why an individual is unable to attend an interview. All claimants must inform the Home Office ahead of time if they are unable to attend. It is not considered reasonable for claimants to continually delay or avoid attending their asylum interview. The interview is an important opportunity to provide information about the reasons someone is seeking protection. Refer to the Withdrawing asylum claims guidance for the timescales claimants have to provide reasons and evidence for their non-attendance.

On receipt of any medical evidence, you must check that it has been compiled by a suitably qualified, relevant, healthcare professional regulated by the GMC, HCPC, NMC or GDC, and consider the evidence to establish when you can rebook the interview or consider whether the interview can be omitted in line with paragraph 339NA of the Immigration Rules.

All requests or decisions to cancel or suspend an asylum interview due to sickness must be signed off by a HEO or SEO and all relevant details must be noted on Home Office records.

Non-attendance for other reasons

If the claimant states that they were unable to attend due to severe travel delays or disruption, they must explain and where necessary provide acceptable evidence of this, for example, information from the travel company or news reports of severe disruption. For wide-scale travel disruption known to the Home Office it may also be evident without the need to request specific evidence. You must consider whether any explanation for non-attendance is reasonable.

The Home Office may also cancel interviews in advance if they become aware ahead of time of widespread disruption (for example, national strikes). These interviews will be rescheduled as soon as possible.

You must not accept explanations such as the unavailability of the immigration adviser to meet with the claimant before the interview, unavailability of their immigration adviser or interpreter for the scheduled interview, attendance at college or, where permission to work has been granted, employment commitments.

Treat the claim as withdrawn because of non-attendance

If the claimant does not attend and no explanation is received within the timescales set out in the Withdrawing asylum claims guidance, or the response received does not evidence that they failed to attend due to circumstances beyond their control, or contact is lost and the immigration adviser is unable to assist, you should normally treat the claim as withdrawn and stop considering it, in line with paragraph 333C of the Immigration Rules. For further advice see guidance on withdrawing asylum claims.

Pending prosecutions

If a claimant is awaiting an interview and checks reveal there is a pending prosecution, Home Office staff will need to decide whether to proceed with an interview, or whether to immediately put the case on hold and delay interviewing until the outcome of the pending prosecution is known. In general, interviews should not normally be delayed while awaiting the outcome of a pending prosecution even if the subsequent asylum decision will need to be paused to await the prosecution outcome.

If you believe there is a reason why the interview should be delayed, you must discuss this with your SCW and obtain agreement to put the case on hold. This is because, even if the case is subsequently paused at the decision-making stage, it is important that processing can resume as soon as the outcome of the pending prosecution is known. Further information is available in the Pending prosecutions in asylum claims guidance.

Choice of language

Asylum interviews must be conducted in a language that the claimant can communicate in to a sufficient level for the purpose of the asylum interview.

Before inviting the claimant to attend an asylum interview, you must review all available evidence to determine the language that the interview should be conducted in.

A claimant may have been screened in one language but expressed a preference for the asylum interview to be conducted in another language.

If you cannot find an interpreter in their preferred language, you may use an interpreter who speaks the language used at the screening interview or another language it is considered there is evidence that the claimant is proficient in. Various factors may demonstrate or indicate proficiency in another language (including English), including where the claimant:

completed a visa application in English

completed a visa application interview in English

entered the UK on an immigration route which required demonstrating proficiency in English

completed a Screening Interview in English

submitted documentation in English

spent time in education in another country where that language was utilised

undertaken a job role in another country where that language was utilised

spent time in the UK to become further accustomed to the English language

requested permission to work whilst an asylum claim is pending in the UK

You must explain this to the claimant and conduct the interview in the language used at the screening interview or the language it is considered the claimant is proficient in, unless the claimant’s command of the language is not good enough for the asylum interview.

Where attempts are made to interview the claimant in another language and it is clear the claimant and interpreter do not understand each other, you should suspend the interview. You should review the case and contact a SCW for advice if necessary. See also languages at interview.

There may be cases where a claimant attends their asylum interview but refuses to complete the interview because we have been unable to source an interpreter in their preferred language. If it is considered that the claimant’s command of another language is good enough to conduct an asylum interview, you must expect the claimant to continue with the interview as arranged. Where the claimant refuses to complete the interview, you must warn them that their asylum claim may be decided based on available evidence, which may result in their asylum claim being refused due to non-compliance under paragraph 339M of the Immigration Rules. Once you have issued this warning, you must give the claimant an opportunity to speak to their immigration adviser if they have one. Where the claimant still refuses to complete the interview, you must suspend the interview. The interview record must include details of the reason why the interview has been suspended and must record any warnings issued to the claimant prior to the suspension.

You should consider all information provided by the claimant in the round. Where a claimant fails to disclose information during an interview, this may impact their credibility adversely. But this is not an automatic finding, as there might be mitigating or compelling circumstances which you might need to consider.

Policy objective

The policy objective when you conduct an asylum interview is to gather enough evidence to be able to fairly and properly consider and determine the claim. You must:

provide a positive and secure environment to support the claimant to disclose all evidence, including sensitive information to support their claim

ensure that all asylum claimants are treated with respect, dignity and fairness regardless of their:

age

disability

ethnicity

nationality

race

gender

sexual orientation

religion or belief

ask appropriate, open and focused questions to encourage full disclosure and gather relevant evidence on important aspects of the claim – this will allow you to:

create an environment in which the claimant is able to present their case as fully as possible, to enable you to ascertain and evaluate the information they provide

assess the credibility of the claimant’s statements

give the claimant an opportunity to explain anything that appears to be implausible or inconsistent

identify any vulnerable claimants and safeguarding issues and make the relevant referrals to the Safeguarding Hub to enable signposting to appropriate support services for example, where there are concerns over physical and mental health, the claimant has experienced torture, sexual or domestic violence, or modern slavery, or there are child protection concerns

Asylum interviews: best interests of the child

Section 55 of the Borders, Citizenship and Immigration Act 2009 requires the Home Office to carry out its functions in a way that takes into account the need to safeguard and promote the welfare of children in the UK. In dealing with parents and children, you must see the family both as a unit and as individuals. Although a child’s best interests are not a factor in assessing whether a fear of persecution is well-founded, the way that you interact with children throughout the interview and the decision-making process, and any decisions following the determination of refugee status must take account of the section 55 duty.

You must comply with this duty when carrying out actions set out in this instruction in respect of children and those with children. You must follow the principles set out in the statutory guidance Every Child Matters - Change for Children.

Our statutory duty to children means you must demonstrate:

fair treatment which meets the same standard a British child would receive

the child’s best interests being a primary, although not the only, consideration

no discrimination of any kind

timely processing of asylum claims

identification of those who might be at risk from harm

Considering claims from those who are under eighteen must be conducted by decision-makers who have completed the requisite training and are qualified to interview and decide them. See Processing children’s asylum claims.

Even if a separate claim is not being made, it is important not to lose sight of the child as an individual, as well as part of a family, to be vigilant and responsive to their protection and welfare needs and to consider how this could impact on the needs of the family as a whole.

On 19 March 2021 the UK Supreme Court in G (Appellant) v G (Respondent) [2021]

UKSC 9 found that a child who is named as a dependant on an asylum claim can and should (generally) be understood to have made a claim for asylum in their own right. This means that child dependants must be treated as asylum claimants unless they do not have protection needs.

When a child is included as a dependant on an asylum claim, the main claimant is asked to explain whether that child has protection needs, and if they do, whether these are the same as, or additional or different to why the main claimant is claiming asylum.

Where a child has the same protection needs as that of the main claimant (their parent), they are considered to be an asylum claimant in their own right, but their asylum claim can be considered as part of a Family Asylum Claim. This means that the asylum claims of the main claimant and any dependent children with the same protection needs will be decided within a single consideration, using evidence provided by the main claimant. For further information, see the Family Asylum Claims guidance.

Where a child has additional or different protection needs to that of the main claimant, they are considered to be an asylum claimant in their own right, but their asylum claim cannot be considered as part of a Family Asylum Claim. Nor can the child be treated as a dependant on the asylum claim of the main claimant (their parent). The child’s claim must be considered as that of an accompanied asylum-seeking child, in accordance with the guidance on Processing children’s asylum claims.

Where a child does not have protection needs, they may continue to be treated as a dependant on the asylum claim of the main claimant.

There may be occasions where at the time of the asylum interview, it is unclear whether a dependent child has protection needs of their own. Where this is the case, you must ask the main claimant whether the child has protection needs and if so, whether they are the same as, additional or different to why they themselves are claiming asylum. Refer to the Family Asylum Claims guidance for detailed instructions on how to establish a child’s protection needs during a main claimant’s asylum interview.
